---
title: "Native API"
---

This page describes EvoDAG's own classes: `EvoDAGE` (the ensemble),
`EvoDAG.model.EvoDAG` (a single model), the search engine `RGP` and the
`Model` and `Ensemble` objects that their fits return. They are not
deprecated and they do not need scikit-learn. The scikit-learn classes of the
[Python](python.qmd) page are the usual way to use EvoDAG; they are built on
the same code and fit the same models.

Use the native API when you:

* work with the models that the [command line](cli.qmd) stores, which are
  `Model` and `Ensemble` objects;
* need what only `EvoDAGE` offers: a `time_limit` for the whole ensemble,
  `tmpdir` to resume an interrupted fit, a `test_set` evaluated along the
  evolution, or `max_training_size`;
* have code that already uses these classes, which keeps working.

The two forms are equivalent. With the same parameters, seed and labels
they fit the same models, and the regression predictions and the
`decision_function` (the median over the members) are identical. The one
difference is the `predict` of the classification ensemble: `EvoDAGE` returns
the class chosen by most members, whereas `EnsembleClassifier` returns the
class with the largest median `decision_function` (the sign of it with two
classes), so that `predict`, `decision_function` and `predict_proba` agree, as
scikit-learn expects. The two rules coincide on most examples, not on all of
them.

| Native API | scikit-learn classes |
|:-----------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|
| `EvoDAGE(n_estimators=n, seed=s, **kw)` | `EnsembleClassifier(EvoDAGClassifier(**kw), n_estimators=n, random_state=s)` |
| `EvoDAGE(n_estimators=n, seed=s, classifier=False, **kw)` | `EnsembleRegressor(EvoDAGRegressor(**kw), n_estimators=n, random_state=s)` |
| `EvoDAG.model.EvoDAG(seed=s, **kw)` | `EvoDAGClassifier(random_state=s, **kw)` |
| `EvoDAG.model.EvoDAG(seed=s, classifier=False, **kw)` | `EvoDAGRegressor(random_state=s, **kw)` |

In the scikit-learn classes the keywords `kw` that are not `popsize`,
`early_stopping_rounds` or `time_limit` go in `params={...}`, and the labels
may be anything (the native classes want numbers).

Every Python block on this page is executed by the test suite of the
repository (`tests/test_docs.py`). The blocks share state: each one builds on
the variables of the previous one, so you can paste the whole page into a
script.

## Which class do I use?

There are three entry points, and the name `EvoDAG` is used by two of them.

| Import | What it is |
|:------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| `from EvoDAG import EvoDAGE` | the **ensemble** with a `fit` / `predict` interface |
| `from EvoDAG.model import EvoDAG` | a **single model** with the same interface |
| `from EvoDAG import EvoDAG` (also `RGP`, `RootGP`) | the **search engine** that runs one evolution; you get the fitted model with `.model()` |

`Model` and `Ensemble` (what the fits return) are also importable from the
top-level package: `from EvoDAG import Model, Ensemble`.

## Data

`X` is a two-dimensional array with one row per example, or anything NumPy
can turn into one (a list of lists, for instance). For classification `y`
holds the class of each example as numbers, and the predictions are given
back in the same numbers; they need not be consecutive. Strings as labels
are not accepted by these classes (the [command line](cli.qmd) maps them to
numbers for you, and the classes of the [Python](python.qmd) page accept them). For regression `y` holds the real targets.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.randn(200, 5)
# three classes, labelled 1, 5 and 9
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] ** 2 > 1).astype(int) + (X[:, 2] > 1.0)
y = np.array([1, 5, 9])[y]
```

## Classification with an ensemble

`EvoDAGE` trains `n_estimators` independent EvoDAG runs. Each run gets its
own seed (`seed`, `seed + 1`, ...), and therefore its own random split of the
training data into the part used to evolve and the validation part used to
stop (see [How it works](how-it-works.qmd)). `n_jobs` is the number of
processes used to train the members and to evaluate them later.

```python
from EvoDAG import EvoDAGE

ensemble = EvoDAGE(n_estimators=5, n_jobs=1, popsize=100,
                   early_stopping_rounds=100, seed=0).fit(X, y)
hy = ensemble.predict(X)
print("accuracy:", (hy == y).mean())
```

Any keyword that is not an argument of `EvoDAGE` is a parameter of the
evolution (here `popsize` and `early_stopping_rounds`); all of them are
listed in [Parameters](parameters.qmd).

`fit` returns the fitted `EvoDAG.Ensemble`, which has these methods:

| Method | Returns |
|:---------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `predict(X)` | the class of each row: the class chosen by most members |
| `predict_proba(X)` | one row per example, one column per class: the fraction of members that voted for each class |
| `decision_function(X)` | the median over the members of the raw outputs, one column per class |
| `raw_decision_function(X)` | the raw outputs of every member side by side, with `n_estimators * n_classes` columns |
| `models` | the list of `Model` objects, one per member |

The columns follow the sorted class labels, which are
`np.unique(y)`.

```python
proba = ensemble.predict_proba(X)
print(proba.shape, proba.sum(axis=1)[:3])

scores = ensemble.decision_function(X)
print(scores.shape)

raw = ensemble.raw_decision_function(X)
print(raw.shape)
print(len(ensemble.models), "members")
```

For classification a model has one output per class: the problem is solved
one class against the others, and `predict` picks the class with the largest
output. When the last node of a model is a Naive Bayes or a Nearest Centroid
node its outputs are squashed into the interval from -1 to 1 before they are
returned; for any other kind of node they are the raw values.

## Classification with a single model

`EvoDAG.model.EvoDAG` fits one run. It takes the same keywords as the
ensemble, without `n_estimators`, `n_jobs` and `tmpdir`. After `fit` the fitted model is in the
`model` attribute.

```python
from EvoDAG.model import EvoDAG as SingleEvoDAG

single = SingleEvoDAG(popsize=100, early_stopping_rounds=100, seed=0).fit(X, y)
print("accuracy:", (single.predict(X) == y).mean())

model = single.model
print("nodes:", model.size, "height:", model.height)
print("validation fitness:", model.fitness_vs)
```

`decision_function` of a single model returns a list with one array per
class, instead of one two-dimensional array. `model.fitness_vs` is the
fitness on the validation part, and it is the *negative* of the error: zero
is perfect and lower values are worse.

## Regression

Pass `classifier=False`. The defaults for regression come from a different
file, `default_parameters_r.json`, and `predict` returns the real values. That
file has the ordinary selections (a tournament on fitness for the arguments and
a negative tournament for the individual that leaves), not the agreement
selection that is the default of classification.

```python
yr = 2 * X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] ** 2 + 0.1 * rng.randn(200)

regressor = EvoDAGE(n_estimators=5, classifier=False, popsize=100,
                    early_stopping_rounds=100, seed=0).fit(X, yr)
hr = regressor.predict(X)
print("correlation:", np.corrcoef(hr, yr)[0, 1])
```

In regression the ensemble prediction is the median of the members'
predictions. A regression with several targets at once is possible: pass
`multiple_outputs=True` and a list with one array per target as `y`;
`predict` then returns one column per target.

## Choosing the function set and other parameters

The functions that EvoDAG may use to build an individual are parameters,
named after the function. A boolean switches the function on or off; an
integer sets how many arguments it takes, and `0` removes it. Everything else
is an ordinary keyword.

```python
tuned = EvoDAGE(n_estimators=3, popsize=100, early_stopping_rounds=100,
                Mul=0, Sin=False, Add=10, tournament_size=3,
                seed=0).fit(X, y)
print((tuned.predict(X) == y).mean())
```

You can also start from a JSON file of your own with `params_fname`; the
format is described in [Parameters](parameters.qmd). Keywords given in the
call override what the file says.

## Looking inside a model

A fitted `Model` is a list of nodes stored in evaluation order. It can tell
how big it is, which input variables it ended up using, and it can write
itself in the dot language of Graphviz.

```python
import io

print("inputs used (variable: times):", dict(model.inputs()))

dot = io.StringIO()
model.graphviz(dot)
print(dot.getvalue().splitlines()[0])
```

`model.graphviz("model.dot")` writes the same text to a file, and
`model.graphviz(fpt, terminals=False)` leaves the input variables out. With
Graphviz installed, `dot -Tsvg model.dot -o model.svg` draws it. In the
picture below the node at the top (green) is the output; the red nodes are
the ones at height zero, which are the inputs and the functions applied
directly to them; the blue ones are internal nodes, darker the higher they
are.

![A model fitted to a small synthetic problem. Generated by `website/figures/make_figures.py`.](../figures/dag.svg)

For an ensemble, `ensemble.graphviz("directory")` writes one file per
member into that directory.

## Saving and loading

Models and ensembles are plain Python objects and can be pickled. The
command line tools store their models with `pickle` inside a gzip file.

```python
import pickle

blob = pickle.dumps(ensemble)
restored = pickle.loads(blob)
print((restored.predict(X) == hy).all())
```

## Running one evolution yourself

The search engine is what the classes above are built on. `RGP.init` reads
the default parameters, `fit` runs the evolution and `model()` returns the
fitted model. You can also reach the population it evolved.

```python
from EvoDAG import RGP

engine = RGP.init(popsize=100, early_stopping_rounds=100, seed=0)
engine.fit(X, y)
best = engine.model()
print(type(best).__name__, "predictions:", best.predict(X)[:5])
print("individuals created:", len(engine.population.hist))
```

`engine.model()` returns the early stopping individual: the one with the
best fitness on the validation part. `engine.model(v)` returns the model of
any individual `v` found in `engine.population.hist`.
